Towards a Community-Driven Validation Framework for
AI/ML Methods in Volcano Monitoring

svg.text: Yannik Behr1, Conny Hammer2, Matthias Ohrnberger3 · ¹Earth Sciences New Zealand · ²Universität Hamburg · 3Universität Potsdam

tspan.tspan: Uptake of AI/ML methods in volcano monitoring lags behind

text.tspan: research, mainly because of three structural challenges:

svg.text: Benchmarking datasets propelled progress in CV and NLP, but none exist

text.tspan: Missing implementation standards make methods hard to reproduce and
compare.

svg.text: Many approaches remain deterministic, favouring overconfident models and
complicating integration into probabilistic, risk-based decision frameworks.

text.tspan: Successful validation frameworks exist in earth sciences (CSEP/floatCSEP for earthquake
forecasting1; seisbench for seismology2). Our requirements build on these but account for the larger
diversity of data types in volcano monitoring.

svg.text: The framework is packaged so that

text.tspan: A researcher should be able to submit a
model with minimal boilderplate and be free
to choose their development framework
Given the diversity of data types and methodologies
in volcano monitoring, tight integration and
standardisation may not be feasible. Instead, we
propose workflow tools to capture reproducible
computational pipelines — providing reproducible
environments, decentralised execution, and
seamless transition from testing to operations.
Wrapping workflows in a Python package adds
common processing steps and a low barrier to entry.
We demonstrate this with two eruption forecasting
pipelines for Whakaari/White Island implemented as
a Snakemake workflow (Figure 2) within a Python
package: one pipeline uses Bayesian Networks with
multiple data types3, and the other uses Random
Forests and RSAM4 .

• A common validation framework can accelerate progress as it
already has in earthquake forecasting and seismology.
• The goal is not to pick winners, but to identify the right algorithm
for each data situation and to build trust.
• We are planning a workshop at IAVCEI 2027 (Incheon,
SouthKorea). If you are interested to participate scan the QR
code to send us an email.

The two models are conceptually different.
The Bayesian Network integrates five data
streams within a simple model structure; low-
frequency airborne gas sampling produces
slow-changing, longer-horizon forecasts.
The Random Forest uses only RSAM but
derives a rich feature set, yielding much
shorter-term forecasts (Figure 3). For volcano
monitoring, the key point is True Posive Rate
= 1, where no events are missed.
